statement: Nine people sit around a round table. Each is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. At least one of them is a knight. Every one of them says: "Exactly one of my two neighbours is a knave." How many knights are at the table?

choices.misconception: I found that a table of only knaves works and did not use the fact that at least one person is a knight.
I found the right pattern but counted the knaves instead of the knights.
I seated one knave among eight knights and checked only the two knights sitting next to the knave.
I took everyone's statement as true without checking that someone would then have to be a knave.

hints: Start with a knight. What must its two neighbours be?

Each knight has one knight and one knave beside it. A knave's sentence is false, so its neighbours are both knights or both knaves. Build the seating around the table from one knight and see what repeats.
Next to a knight sit one knight and one knave. Those two knights then need a knave on their other sides, so the pattern knight, knight, knave starts repeating.

solutions.reliable: Take a knight K. One neighbour is a knave and the other a knight, say K K N. The second knight also needs exactly one knave beside it, so its other neighbour is a knave: N K K N. A knave cannot have exactly one knave beside it, and it already has a knight on one side, so its other neighbour is a knight too. The seating repeats knight, knight, knave, and 9 seats hold three full blocks, so the pattern closes up correctly. Check: each knight has one knight and one knave beside it (true), and each knave has two knights beside it, so its sentence is false. That gives 6 knights. A table with no knights also fits (each knave has two knave neighbours), but the question says there is at least one knight. The transferable idea: in truth-teller puzzles, fix one person's type, follow what it forces, and check the pattern closes up round the circle.

whyOnTest: Knights-and-knaves puzzles test chasing consequences: one knight forces a repeating block, and the circle must close up exactly.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
